title_en: Rich Friedman on the Rise of Private Markets and AI Investing
title_zh: Rich Friedman 谈私募股权的崛起与 AI 投资
subtitle_zh: Goldman Sachs Asset Management 主席 Rich Friedman 回顾 45 年商户银行建设史
summary_zh: 本期 Goldman Sachs Exchanges 的 Great Investors 系列由 Allison Moss 对话 Goldman Sachs 资产管理主席、另类投资领域领军人物 Rich Friedman，回顾他四十五年的商户银行（merchant bank）建设史。Friedman 记得入职第一天在 55 Broad Street 八楼，整组只有二三十人；同一天 Salomon Brothers 被卖给 Phibro。他最初做私募融资与信贷融资，因在 Citibank 资产抵押贷款（asset-based lending）部门工作过，成为少数有这类经验的人，被派去为早期杠杆收购充当财务顾问、协助募集债务。1990 年他成为合伙人并遇到新导师 Hank Paulson，此前刚亲历由储贷危机造成的第一次衰退；当时还没有“商户银行”概念，这条路径孕育出自营投资部门（principal investment area），1992 年募集首只 GS Capital Partners 基金。2000 年前后执行办公室要求他组建团队布局科技，尽管团队本能抗拒、认为科技陌生且像掷骰子，他们仍派最精明的投资人去摸底；他总结出一条纪律——在动量（momentum）时期保持克制、待在自己擅长的领域，因为追在顶端历史上并不成功，那波科技与电信热潮中基金只投了五六亿美元。他回忆 2008 年 Goldman 的存亡时刻，市场普遍认为债务融资之墙不会形成、每笔私募股权投资都会失败，而事实并非如此；他不止一次被迫向整个组合喊话“关紧舱盖”。谈到今天的私募股权行业，他直言已经工业化、有几百家机构，当前的危机在于退出（exits）而非经营表现，但搜寻、发现、管理并创造价值仍是了不起的生意。他还谈到多年固定篮球局带来的团队启示、组织里未变的自豪感与协作，以及 Richard Rainwater 给他的激励；最后坦言这是个充满挑战、令人不安却不乏味的时期，人们的乐观未必按预想的时间表兑现。
description: Rich Friedman on the Rise of Private Markets and AI Investing

turns.en: I never imagined the PE industry would evolve into what it is. This is industrialized, there are hundreds and hundreds of them. Thousands. Thousands.
turns.zh: 我从没想过 PE（私募股权，private equity）行业会演变成今天这个样子。这是工业化了，有几百几千家。几千家。几千家。

turns.en: You know, the crisis today in the PE industry is exits. It's not operating performance. Everything's slowed. Yep. Let's put it that way. But it's an incredible business to be able to go search, find, and then manage and create.
turns.zh: 你知道，PE 行业今天的危机是退出（exits）。不是经营表现。一切都慢了下来。是的。就这么说吧。但这是一门了不起的生意——能去搜寻、发现，然后管理、创造价值。

turns.en: And the question is, is that still doable in the world? And my answer would be yes. Welcome to Goldman Sachs Exchange's Great Investors. Today, I sit down with Rich Friedman, the chairman of Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and one of the foremost leaders in alternative investing.
turns.zh: 问题是，在这个世界里这还行得通吗？我的答案是：行得通。欢迎来到 Goldman Sachs Exchanges 的《Great Investors》。今天，我与 Rich Friedman 对坐长谈——他是 Goldman Sachs 资产管理（Asset Management）的主席，也是另类投资（alternative investing）领域最重要的领军人物之一。

turns.en: Well, welcome to Great Investors Rich. It's so great to have you here. Thanks, Allison. This is really a treat for me. So today, I'm interviewing you for Great Investors podcast.
turns.zh: 好，欢迎来到《Great Investors》，Rich，太高兴请到你了。谢谢你，Allison，这对我来说真是种享受。所以今天，我要为《Great Investors》播客采访你。

turns.en: But before we begin that and talk about the investment environment, I want to go back to your start at Goldman Sachs, which is 45 years ago.
turns.zh: 但在开始聊投资环境之前，我想先回到你四十五年前刚进 Goldman Sachs 的时候。

turns.en: Tell us about your first day. What was that like? Do you remember? You know, I do remember. I remember we were at 55 Broad Street. Most people think we were at 85 Broad Street.
turns.zh: 说说你的第一天吧，那是什么感觉？还记得吗？嗯，我确实记得。我们当时在 55 Broad Street，大多数人都以为是在 85 Broad Street。

turns.en: But, you know, I'm dating myself, but I would think I was on the eighth floor. And it was a small area, and there were about 25 to 30 people in the group.
turns.zh: 你知道，说这些我把自己都问老了，但我记得我大概是在八楼。那一小片区域，整个组大概有二十五到三十个人。

turns.en: And the funny thing is, one of the people I saw as I was walking in was this guy named Joel Beckman. He was someone I grew up with in Riverdale.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，我走进去时看到的人里，有个叫 Joel Beckman 的家伙，他是我在 Riverdale 一起长大的。

turns.en: It was a very low key, very welcome in place. And I didn't feel, you know, so anxious walking in there because I knew someone, and it seemed like a, you know, a place you could sort of like assimilate into.
turns.zh: 那是一个非常低调、非常受欢迎的地方。我走进去时没那么紧张，因为里面我认识人，感觉像是一个你可以慢慢融入的地方。

turns.en: So what was it like to work at the firm in the 80s? What was that first, you know, 10 years like? Well, it varied a lot over 10 years, but certainly the early years.
turns.zh: 那在八十年代在这家公司工作是什么感觉？头十年是什么样的？嗯，头十年变化很大，但尤其是最初那几年。

turns.en: But first of all, the day I joined the firm, Salmon Brothers was sold to Fibro. Wow. Now, I didn't say wow because I didn't really know that much about Goldman Sachs or Salmon Brothers, but it was a little bit of a wow that literally, you know, you're joining Goldman Sachs and then you hear that one of its principal competitors were sold.
turns.zh: 首先，我进公司那天，Salomon Brothers 被卖给了 Phibro。哇。我说'哇'其实是因为我当时对 Goldman Sachs 或 Salomon Brothers 了解并不多，但确实有点'哇'——你刚加入 Goldman Sachs，就听说它的一个主要竞争对手被卖掉了。

turns.en: And I think it was sold for like $800 million. It sounded like a lot of money back then, but obviously not so much, you know, today. But, you know, I'd say that we, I got going relatively quickly.
turns.zh: 我记得好像是卖了八亿美元左右。在当时听起来是笔大钱，但显然放到今天就不算多了。我会说我很快就上手了。

turns.en: The group I joined was a group that did private financings, credit debt financings, these financings, and so they were projects. It wasn't advisory.
turns.zh: 我加入的那个组做的是私募融资、信贷融资这类融资，都是一个个项目，不是顾问业务。

turns.en: So what was happening was I was being assigned, you know, to work on different things. Early on in my career, though, I was starting to get assigned to work on some of these early-stage buyouts where we were like financial advisor to help raise the debt.
turns.zh: 所以我当时是被派去参与不同的事。不过职业生涯早期，我就开始被安排去做一些早期的杠杆收购（buyout），我们充当财务顾问，帮他们去募集债务。

turns.en: I had a little experience because in between my years at business school, I worked for Citibank in their asset-based lending area. So I learned about asset-based financings for receivables, for inventory, and the earliest of days of bootstrap LBO people.
turns.zh: 我在这方面有点经验，因为在读商学院的间隙，我在 Citibank 的资产抵押贷款（asset-based lending）部门工作过。所以我了解了针对应收账款、存货的资产抵押贷款，还有最早那一代白手起家的 LBO 玩家。

turns.en: So, you know, I was one of the only ones who had that kind of experience. So when we started to get a few assignments in this, you know, I was chosen to get involved with it, which was, you know, which to me was very interesting.
turns.zh: 所以我是少数有这类经验的人之一。当我们在这一块接到一些委托时，就被选中参与进来，这对我来说非常有意思。

turns.en: You know, I would say that I got assigned very quickly to, you know, we were progressing fast into the LBO world back then. It wasn't called private equity.
turns.zh: 我会说我很快就被派到相关项目上，那时候我们正快速进入 LBO（杠杆收购）的世界。那时候还不叫私募股权。

turns.en: I ended up being assigned to getting involved with a fair amount of media transactions. And it wasn't because I knew anything about it other than I watched TV and read the newspapers.
turns.zh: 我最后被安排参与了不少媒体行业的交易，而原因并不是我对媒体懂多少——无非就是看电视、读报纸。

turns.en: But I became an expert having worked on some of the early recaps in the media industry in the early 80s. Multimedia's recapitalization that Jack Ken Cook came after, a hard hang.
turns.zh: 但我成了专家，因为在八十年代初我做过媒体行业早期的一些再融资（recap），比如 Multimedia 的资本重组，后来 Jack Ken Cook 也做过类似的，很硬的一单。

turns.en: So there were companies that I was involved with early on that were media-related but were transactional, which really fit, you know, sort of my skill base at the time.
turns.zh: 所以我早期参与的一些公司虽然和媒体相关，但都是交易性质的，这正好契合我当时擅长的技能。

turns.en: And you eventually got your battlefield promotion, as you call it. Tell us about that story. So the battlefield promotion was something because this was in the middle of, you know, the first recession that I was sort of, that we were living through, which was in 1989, 1990.
turns.zh: 而你最终得到了你所说的'战场晋升'（battlefield promotion）。讲讲那个故事吧。所以那次战场晋升之所以发生，是因为那正处在——你知道——我亲历的第一次衰退之中，也就是 1989、1990 年。

turns.en: And it was, it felt pretty severe at the time. And this is from the SNL crisis that really, you know, caused this. And I had become partner in 1990, and I was like slated to raise a new buyout fund.
turns.zh: 当时感觉很严重。这在很大程度上是储贷危机（S&L crisis）造成的。我在 1990 年成了合伙人，正准备去募集一只新的收购基金（buyout fund）。

turns.en: And then I met this individual named Hank Paulson, who became my new mentor, who they said, this is who you're going to report to. Because at that point, we were all in investment banking.
turns.zh: 然后我遇到了一个叫 Hank Paulson 的人，他成了我的新导师，他们告诉我：这就是你将来要汇报的对象。因为到那时候，我们都还在投资银行里。

turns.en: There was no concept of a merchant bank. And it was the beginning pathway on to the creation of what we refer to as the principal investment area when we raised our first GS Capital Partners Fund in 1992.
turns.zh: 当时还没有'商户银行'（merchant bank）这个概念。那正是后来所称的'自营投资部门'（principal investment area）开始萌芽的路径——我们在 1992 年募集了第一只 GS Capital Partners 基金。

turns.en: Yeah. And the rest is history. And I'm still alive to tell the story. That's fascinating. What a great experience. I'll tell you, a funny thing about it is that, you know, again, it was just like 20 of us, maybe even less at the time, think about what's going on.
turns.zh: 是的。之后的故事你们都知道了。而我还活着把它讲出来。太引人入胜了，多棒的经历。我告诉你，有意思的是——当时也就二十来个人，甚至更少——你想想那是什么规模。

turns.en: So we sat there and we said, well, what should we call ourselves? And we had some pretty creative people there in terms of promotion, like we call ourselves.
turns.zh: 我们就坐在那儿说：我们该叫什么名字？在起名这块，我们那儿有些挺有创意的人。

turns.en: We should be the principal investment area. We can't be principal investment group. That's not going to be a good acronym. And then we said, maybe we should be the principal investment division.
turns.zh: 我们该叫自营投资部门（principal investment area）。不能叫 principal investment group，那缩写不好。然后我们又说，要不叫 principal investment division 吧。

turns.en: And so I took that up to Steve Freedman. He basically says, yeah, I don't really think you're ready to become a division of those. But we had a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 于是我把这事汇报给 Steve Friedman。他基本上说：嗯，我觉得你们还没准备好成为一个 division。不过我们玩得很开心。

turns.en: And we actually, you know, we created the business and we created the principal investment area, which today still has what I'll call brand value in the marketplace.
turns.zh: 而实际上，我们开创了这门业务，创建了 principal investment area——直到今天，它在我所说的市场里仍然有品牌价值。

turns.en: That is extraordinary. So you've talked about mentorship. It was a big part of why you decided to take the initial risk and build up a team at the firm in media and communications.
turns.zh: 那真是非凡。你谈到过导师制，这也是当初你决定承担首要风险、在公司里为媒体与通信业务组建团队的重要原因。

turns.en: How did you lean on your mentors throughout your career and in what ways did they help guide you? It's a good question because I never thought of them as mentors, but they were.
turns.zh: 在你的整个职业生涯里，你是如何依靠你的导师的？他们在哪些方面给了你指引？这是个好问题，因为我从没把他们当成导师，但他们其实就是。

turns.en: And so it was a smaller place back then. And if you distinguish yourselves in ways you could get identified. So early on, I was identified by one individual and he was the one who asked me to, you know, build and create the media and communications banking business in 1987.
turns.zh: 那时候公司还小。如果你在某些方面脱颖而出，就会被注意到。所以很早就有一位前辈看中了我，正是他在 1987 年让我去创建媒体与通信银行业务。

turns.en: And I was really reticent about that because this was a client service business. You know, at that point, I'm 33, 34 years old, not even. And I'm like, wait a minute, my clients are these CFOs and CEOs of these big companies like ABC, Capsities, these people in their fifties or sixties.
turns.zh: 我当时其实挺不情愿，因为那是一门客户服务业务。你知道，那年我才三十三、三十四岁，还不算呢。我会想：等等，我的客户是这些大公司的 CFO 和 CEO——比如 ABC、CapCities 这些人，他们都五六十岁了。

turns.en: I don't think I could be successful, you know, covering them. And this isn't what my strength is. And, you know, he convinced me that ultimately this would be a stretch assignment and that, you know, it wasn't going to last forever, but I would learn a lot of things.
turns.zh: 我觉得我去覆盖他们未必能成功，这不是我的强项。但他说服了我：这终究是一次拉伸性的任务（stretch assignment），不会永远这样，但我会学到很多东西。

turns.en: And so he said, you know, do it. So I came back and got excited, you know, and did it. At each of these sort of stages in my career, it was a little bit of fate.
turns.zh: 于是他说：去做吧。我就回来，变得兴奋起来，把它做成了。在我职业生涯的每一个这样的阶段，都有一点命运的意味。

turns.en: I wasn't looking for anyone. And our mentoring program and support programs at the firm now, we didn't have them back then. And what I learned, Allison, early on in the creation of, you know, the Merchant Bank was, it was a fragile business model for the firm.
turns.zh: 我并没有刻意去找谁。公司现在的导师项目和支持项目，那时候我们根本没有。而我很早学到的、在创建商户银行过程中的一个体会是——对这家公司来说，这是一种脆弱的商业模式。

turns.en: It wasn't central to the firm's advisory and trading businesses. And there was some long history of, let's, I'll use the word mistakes. And that for this to be successful, I needed, I really did need a big brother, you know, watching what we were doing, advising what we're doing and protecting.
turns.zh: 它并不处于公司咨询和交易业务的核心。有一段很长的历史，我就用'失误'这个词吧——而要让这件事成功，我真的需要一位'大哥'（big brother）在看着我们在做什么、给我们建议、保护我们。

turns.en: And that was critical in the early days to create this. So it was important to me at every next stage, even as a very, let's call it rising senior partner of the firm, I needed support from the executive office.
turns.zh: 所以在开创的早期，这一点至关重要。正因如此，在我之后的每一个阶段——哪怕身为公司里所谓崛起中的资深合伙人——我都需要执行办公室（executive office）的支持。

turns.en: So it did take four or five decades to really build the Merchant Bank into what we know it as today. And you did it in a very deliberate way.
turns.zh: 所以确实花了四五十年，才真正把商户银行建成我们今天所知的样子。而你是以一种非常深思熟虑的方式做到的。

turns.en: So what were some of the milestones along the way as you built the Merchant Bank? So the first milestone, I obviously was raising GSCP-1. That was a billion dollar fund in 1992.
turns.zh: 那在你建设商户银行的过程中，有哪些里程碑？第一个里程碑，显然就是我募集 GSCP-1，那是 1992 年一只十亿美元的基金。

turns.en: And at that point, there were only five firms that had joined our funds. So that was a signature thing at that point. And then we had some signature deals, like buying in a 28.5% stake in Polo Ralph Lauren.
turns.zh: 在那个时点，只有五家机构加入了我们的基金。所以那在当时是一件标志性的大事。之后我们又做了几笔标志性交易，比如买下 Polo Ralph Lauren 28.5% 的股权。

turns.en: And some other deals that we did became, you know, branded deals for us. And then we built the private equity business through the, you know, mid-90s.
turns.zh: 还有一些我们做的交易，成了给我们贴上品牌标签的交易。然后我们在九十年代中期把私募股权业务一步步做大。

turns.en: Just, you know, basically getting bigger, raising a bigger fund, nothing too special. And in the late 90s, I came up with the idea that we should raise a subordinated debt fund.
turns.zh: 基本上就是越做越大、募集更大的基金，没什么特别轰动的。到九十年代末，我萌生了一个想法：我们应该募集一只次级债基金（subordinated debt fund）。

turns.en: And it was really, the first thought was, it's really for European deals. Because Europe didn't have the ability to raise subordinated debt for their buyouts.
turns.zh: 最初的想法是——这主要是为欧洲交易服务的。因为欧洲没法为他们的收购去募集次级债。

turns.en: That was sort of what the initial idea was. And there was just no private subordinated debt industry at that point in time. So we raised the fund, and we actually ended up having both US, you know, and European deals.
turns.zh: 这就是最初的想法。而当时根本还没有私募次级债这个行业。于是我们募集了基金，最终既做了美国的交易，也做了欧洲的交易。

turns.en: Because we were just, if you will, competing with the US public markets for deals. But that was a step forward in the creation of a credit business inside, you know, the private equity business.
turns.zh: 因为说到底，我们是在和美国的公开市场竞争交易机会。但这一步，是在私募股权业务内部开创信贷业务的一次前进。

turns.en: And that was the business that Moonier said or led for you. Correct. And then, you know, you'll laugh at this because you can see it. As we got into the tech, you know, growth bubble, if you want to call it, in the 2000 era.
turns.zh: 而那块业务是 Monrier 为你掌舵或领导的。对。然后——你听了会笑，因为你能想象得到——当我们进入科技、成长股的那场泡沫（bubble），也就是 2000 年前后。

turns.en: I won't say who, but a message came from the EO that, Rich, we want to see more opportunities in all of these, you know, tech opportunities, and you have to build a team to do it.
turns.zh: 我不说是谁，但执行办公室（EO）传来一句话：Rich，我们要看到这些科技机会里更多的布局，你得组建一支团队来做。

turns.en: And they could tell that we were resisting it because a big part of, you know, my thinking and my team's thinking is, let's stick to what we're good at.
turns.zh: 他们看得出我们在抗拒，因为我和我的团队很大一部分想法是：专注于我们擅长的东西。

turns.en: And tech is a little bit of, you know, for us, we didn't have the people. It just seemed like it was, you know, a roll of the dice. You know, we said, OK, if that's what they want.
turns.zh: 而科技对我们来说有点陌生，我们没有这方面的人，看起来就像是掷骰子。我们说：好吧，如果他们真想这样。

turns.en: So we started to focus on, you know, tech deals. And a lot of the initial funding was really done on balance sheet and with employee funds. So, you know, we were dabbling in it and we had like a matrix.
turns.zh: 于是我们开始关注科技交易。早期的很多投资，其实都是用资产负债表上的钱和员工资金做的。所以我们在浅尝辄止，搞了个矩阵。

turns.en: We could put 3 million in something, 6 million in something, 9 million in something. And it was just like, these were bets. Now, we didn't know that looking back in time that we could at one point own 13% of Alibaba when it was being formed.
turns.zh: 我们可以在某个项目上投三百万，某个投六百万，某个投九百万——这些本质上就是赌注。回想起来我们当时并不知道，有朝一日我们能在 Alibaba 创立之际持有它 13% 的股份。

turns.en: Wow. And if you went back a decade earlier, we owned 10% of Qualcomm. So the firm was pretty phenomenal in bringing opportunities, you know, to us.
turns.zh: 哇。而如果再往前推十年，我们还持有过 Qualcomm 10% 的股份。所以这家公司在把机会送到我们面前这件事上，真是非同凡响。

turns.en: But that was our entry into tech and growth. And that has had its ups and downs and ups and downs. But nonetheless, you know, we're a big growth investor today.
turns.zh: 但那正是我们进入科技与成长的开端。这一路有过起起落落、起起落落。但无论如何，我们今天已经是一家大型的成长型投资人（growth investor）。

turns.en: But that was sort of a seminal thing moving into that. Then I'd say we took a big leap in 2005 by raising a $5 billion fund. And that's when, you know, the whole PE industry was sort of, that was like the Renaissance period, where we were doing deals, as you know, every other week.
turns.zh: 那是迈向那个方向的一个里程碑式的事。之后我要说，我们在 2005 年迈了一大步——募集了一只五十亿美元的基金。那正是整个 PE 行业——你知道——的'文艺复兴'时期，我们几乎每隔一周就在做交易。

turns.en: I think we did 200 billion of buyouts in an 18 month period. It was a crazy period. And it challenged our discipline, if you will, because it was the first time in history where the public markets were saying, we want you private equity to buy us and the valuations were not that crazy.
turns.zh: 我想我们在十八个月里做了两千亿美元的收购。那是一段疯狂的日子。它考验了我们的纪律，因为历史上第一次，公开市场在说：我们希望你们私募股权来收购我们——而估值还不算太疯狂。

turns.en: So, you know, basically, you know, this went on until obviously, you know, the bubble burst. But that was a crazy period. Now, coming out of that period was a big thing, which was we raised a senior debt fund.
turns.zh: 所以这一直持续，直到显然——泡沫破裂。但那真是段疯狂的日子。走出那个时期之后，有一件大事，就是我们募集了一只高级债基金（senior debt fund）。

turns.en: And we raised a real estate debt fund. And these were distress funds that take over the opportunities that were presenting themselves. I never imagined in my career, Allison, that I'd be running a senior debt fund in the Merchant Mag.
turns.zh: 还有一只房地产债基金（real estate debt fund）。这些是困境/特殊机会基金（distress funds），去承接当时冒出来的机会。我在我的职业生涯里从没想过，我会在商户银行里管理一只高级债基金。

turns.en: It's like, really? A library plus two and a half and plus fees. And, you know, but that sort of like filled in that matrix of the portfolio of what businesses are going to win.
turns.zh: 简直难以置信。像 L+2.5、L+2.5 加费用这种。但那确实补全了投资组合的那块矩阵——哪些业务会胜出。

turns.en: You know, Tom Connolly was running it. We made equity like returns in that senior debt vehicle for that first phase. And then it was like pieces to the puzzle.
turns.zh: 那块是 Tom Connolly 在管理。在那个高级债工具的第一阶段，我们做出了类似股权的回报。然后就是一块块拼图归位。

turns.en: Then we raised our first infrastructure fund, you know, right around the same time. So, you know, it happened over time. It wasn't like it happened all at once.
turns.zh: 之后我们在大致同一时间募集了第一只基础设施基金（infrastructure fund）。所以它是随时间逐步发生的，不是一夜之间全到位的。

turns.en: And this was sort of like the PE business kept growing while these new businesses were being added. But we did it at a pace that made sense.
turns.zh: 而且这些新业务在不断加进来的同时，PE 业务也在持续增长。但我们是按照一个合理的节奏在做。

turns.en: And then we did them, let's call it opportunistically in relation to what the market was then presenting ourselves with. I always thought we needed the quality people to run them.
turns.zh: 然后我们做这些事，可以说是在契合当时市场给我们呈现的机会上相机行事。我一直认为，我们需要优秀的人来掌舵这些业务。

turns.en: And we needed to be able to invest them. It wasn't a matter of could we raise the money. It's could we responsibly invest the money. And that's sort of probably why we did it on a slower fashion.
turns.zh: 而且我们要能够把资金投出去。问题不在于我们能不能募到钱，而在于我们能不能审慎地把钱投好。这大概就是我们做得相对慢一些的原因。

turns.en: Maybe we otherwise could. But in these businesses that I've referenced, we were first. So I feel really good about that. The fact that, you know, others have gone past us in the credit side.
turns.zh: 也许本来可以更快。但在我提到的这些业务里，我们都是先行者。所以我对这一点感觉很好。虽然别人在信贷这块后来居上超过我们。

turns.en: But, you know, we're still, you know, top five, let's say, you know, in the credit business, but we were alone. We were, we were top, you know, we were top.
turns.zh: 但我们在信贷业务上仍算是前五、这么说吧——而我们当初是独一无二的。我们是最好的，我们就是最好的。

turns.en: Speaking of being first, we were also the first in Asia. Yes. And overseas investing became a cornerstone, right, of the merchant banking business.
turns.zh: 说到'先行者'，我们在亚洲也是第一家。是的。而海外投资成了商户银行业务的一块基石。

turns.en: What initially prompted you and your team to start looking at Asia, at China, at other overseas investments? When I, you know, got my responsibilities in 92, we immediately built out a few niche funds in Europe.
turns.zh: 最初是什么促使你和你的团队开始看向亚洲、看向中国、看向其他海外投资的？当我在 92 年接手这块职责之后，我们立刻在欧洲搭起了几只细分基金。

turns.en: And we had a business, we had a banking business in Europe. So we had some semblance of a business in Europe to be able to do some deals. The Asia part was, you know, that was different.
turns.zh: 我们在欧洲有一块银行业务，所以在欧洲有一些业务的雏形，可以做些交易。亚洲这块则是另一回事。

turns.en: And I remember that, you know, I took a small, you know, green beret group, we jumped on planes and we went over to, you know, to China. And it was like, where are we?
turns.zh: 我记得，我带了一支小小的'绿色贝雷帽'式突击队，我们跳上飞机去了中国。当时就是：我们在哪儿？

turns.en: What are we doing here? And we, none of us had ever been there before. So these were the first trends, but these were some of the smarter investors we had in my group to try to scope out.
turns.zh: 我们来这儿干什么？我们谁都没去过那里。所以这些是最早的考察——派的是我组里一些最精明的投资人去摸底。

turns.en: Is there stuff that we can do? So of course we're there, like, you know, coming up with like ad hoc ideas about all these bicycles. Hey, I don't see anyone with a bicycle helmet.
turns.zh: 看看有没有我们可以做的事。当然我们到了那儿，就冒出一堆即兴的想法，比如满街的自行车——咦，我没看到任何人戴自行车头盔。

turns.en: Maybe we should invest in bicycle helmet. So we, in the earliest of days, I'd say, we had a skeletal crew of people on the ground and banking was sort of just getting going.
turns.zh: 也许我们该投自行车头盔。所以在最早的日子里，我想我们在地面上只有很少的几个骨干，银行业务也才刚起步。

turns.en: But we did feel as if we had an edge, because as you said, there was nobody else there. And what I found over time is the Chinese welcomed Goldman Sachs and we built a Chinese team.
turns.zh: 但我们确实觉得自己有优势，因为就像你说的，那里还没有别人。而随着时间推移，我发现中国人欢迎 Goldman Sachs，我们还组建了一支中国团队。

turns.en: You know, we built a team that was mostly based in Hong Kong, but eventually we had some based in Shanghai. But we had, we had nationals who were Western trained.
turns.zh: 我们建了一支主要驻扎在香港的团队，但后来也有一些人常驻上海。我们招募的是本土人才，他们受过西方训练。

turns.en: And we felt also had the DNA of a Goldman Sachs person, which is not an easy thing to do. And, you know, Stephanie Hoy, who now runs the business, I remember the first day she joined, and that was 25, 26 years ago.
turns.zh: 我们觉得他们也有 Goldman Sachs 人的那种基因（DNA）——这可不是件容易的事。我还记得 Stephanie Hoy——她如今掌管这块业务——她第一天来上班，那是二十五、二十六年前了。

turns.en: And she understood what the mission was, but we, you know, we built a dedicated team and we had a, you know, we had sort of a targeted focus.
turns.zh: 她理解这个使命是什么。我们组建了一支专职团队，有一个有针对性的聚焦方向。

turns.en: And it took a while before we got ourselves to doing a fair amount of investing there, and it built over time. So the China strategy built over time, and we developed more and more relationships.
turns.zh: 过了好一阵子，我们才做到在那儿进行相当规模的投资，一切是逐步积累起来的。中国的战略就是这样慢慢建起来的，我们发展出越来越多的关系。

turns.en: You know, eventually it, you know, we had that seminal deal, and that was the investment in ICBC. And that was something that no other, you know, US bank or investment bank had the opportunity to do.
turns.zh: 最终我们做了那笔里程碑式的交易，就是对 ICBC（中国工商银行）的投资。那是一种没有其他美国银行或投行有机会做的投资。

turns.en: It was a strategic investment, but the firm made an investment, our funds made an investment. There was a commercial relationship that was established between Goldman Sachs and ICBC.
turns.zh: 那是一笔战略投资，公司也做了投资，我们的基金也做了投资。Goldman Sachs 与 ICBC 之间建立了一种商业关系。

turns.en: It was a very big investment in the privatization, if you will, of the Chinese banks. I think that was probably a seminal moment in us establishing ourselves as constructive investors in China that helped establish ourselves there.
turns.zh: 那是一笔非常大的投资，可以说是推动了中国银行业的私有化。我想，那大概是我们作为建设性投资人（constructive investor）在中国站稳脚跟的一个里程碑时刻，帮助我们在当地建立了地位。

turns.en: The deal industry has always been like one deal leads to three others, and I think that's sort of what happened. But the key thing for me was why I always needed the person at the helm there that I could trust.
turns.zh: 交易这行，一直是一笔交易会带来三笔其他交易，我想大抵就是如此。但对我而言最关键的是——为什么我始终需要在当地有一个我能信赖的人来掌舵。

turns.en: So at first I had Henry Cornell, and then I had Andrew Wolfe, and then Stephanie Hoi. So I had three great investors who I could have a lot of confidence in, because when you go to sleep at night, you know, you're in New York and they're in Hong Kong and they're there.
turns.zh: 所以起初我有 Henry Cornell，然后是 Andrew Wolfe，再然后是 Stephanie Hoi。我有三位我很信得过的优秀投资人，因为当你晚上在纽约入睡时，他们在香港，在那儿。

turns.en: And, you know, they're the ones really sort of doing the on the ground, you know, stuff. So we had great leadership there, and it's continued.
turns.zh: 真正在地面上做事的，是他们。所以我们在那儿有出色的领导力，而且这种传承一直延续下来。

turns.en: So getting back to your career history, you built the principal investing business into a juggernaut. And was there a guiding philosophy as you built up the book and your team?
turns.zh: 回到你的职业经历，你把自营投资业务打造成了一个巨头。在建立起这块业务和团队的过程中，有没有一条指导哲学？

turns.en: It was there a guiding philosophy. Yes, I'll say there were a number of guiding, you know, sort of tenets that we had to have. The first is this business had to work inside Goldman Sachs, and that it wasn't a subsidiary of Goldman Sachs.
turns.zh: 有没有指导哲学——是的，我会说我们有几条必须坚守的信条（tenets）。第一条是：这门业务必须在 Goldman Sachs 内部运转，它不是 Goldman Sachs 的一个子公司。

turns.en: It was a division of Goldman Sachs, and that we needed to have what I'll call is the excellence, the success, and the connectivity no different than the other parts of the firm.
turns.zh: 它是 Goldman Sachs 的一个部门（division），我们需要的，是我所说的卓越、成功，以及与公司的连接——和公司的其他部分没有区别。

turns.en: We needed to be in that patchwork of being part of the firm. So I made sure that along the way we had a lot of connections there. We had good relationships with banking.
turns.zh: 我们需要融入'公司一份子'这块拼图中。所以我确保一路走来我们和公司各处有很多连接，我们和银行业务处好了关系。

turns.en: We also learned to partner with our most important client. Totally. So we needed to have a strategy with our client base and partnering and not competing on a regular basis, because certainly we competed in the marketplace, but not to be in every auction ever created.
turns.zh: 我们也学会了与我们最重要的客户合作。完全同意。所以我们需要针对客户群有一套战略，是合作而非在常态下竞争——我们当然在市场上竞争，但不会去参与每一场竞标。

turns.en: So we needed to have a business strategy that was consistent with the firm strategy, consistent with, you know, the PEs, you know, clients that we had and other clients we had.
turns.zh: 所以我们需要一套业务战略，与公司战略一致，与我们所服务的 PE 客户及其他客户相匹配。

turns.en: So there's a little bit of it's not just the PE firms that could be upset. It could be the other, you know, the other corporates. In terms of the team and the business, Allison, I always believe we needed to be meaningful.
turns.zh: 这里面有一点：不只是 PE 公司可能会不高兴，其他企业客户也可能。在团队和业务上，Allison，我始终认为我们必须是'有分量的'（meaningful）。

turns.en: The team that I, you know, that we built was first class people. And, you know, there would be jokes that, you know, these are really above average astronauts or whatever that, you know, and these are really smart people, successful people, number came from banking and other areas.
turns.zh: 我、我们建起来的这支团队，都是一流的人。人们会开玩笑说，这些都是'远超平均水平的宇航员'之类的——总之都是非常聪明、非常成功的人，有的来自银行业务和其他领域。

turns.en: They wanted to be in a firm where, you know, they felt like they were part of the firm. So this had to be meaningful, scale wise, and it had to be one in which we made a difference that if we were, you know, doing well in our funds, but nobody in the firm knew what's going on.
turns.zh: 他们想在一家公司里，感觉自己就是这家公司的一部分。所以这门业务在规模上必须有分量，必须做到我们能产生影响——如果我们的基金做得很好，但公司里却没人知道发生了什么，

turns.en: That wasn't going to do it for, I think, the large majority of our people. So we kept our people for, I think, pretty long periods of time. We had good retention.
turns.zh: 那对我们大多数同事来说，是不够的。所以我想我们把人留住了相当长的时间，我们有很好的留存率。

turns.en: So that was important. Most important was we had to have good returns. You don't have good returns for nothing else matters. So, you know, the investment process needed to be as high quality as we could make it.
turns.zh: 这一点很重要。而最重要的是我们必须有好的回报。没有好回报，其他一切都不重要。所以投资流程必须做到我们能做到的最高质量。

turns.en: It couldn't be, you know, Rich's, you know, Rich's investment portfolio couldn't be ever, I made all the calls and that was it. It needed to have the integrity and the real essence of, you know, realizing that we're dead.
turns.zh: 它不能变成——你知道——Rich 的投资组合，永远是'我说了算'，就这样。它需要有那种正直和真正的精髓——那种'我们完蛋了'的清醒认知。

turns.en: If we don't have good investment results, we don't have nothing. None of that other stuff will matter if we don't have good investment results.
turns.zh: 如果我们没有好的投资结果，我们就一无所有。其他那些东西，如果没有好的投资结果，全都不作数。

turns.en: So the investment process was always the lifeblood of what we did. And we also made this so that it was, you know, we had so much of an employees capital invested.
turns.zh: 所以投资流程始终是我们所做一切的生命线。我们还做到让员工大量地把自有资金投进来。

turns.en: So there's a little bit of, you know, it's like the employees cared. We're all rooting for you. Exactly. We're rooting for us. We're supportive.
turns.zh: 所以多少有一种——员工也在乎的感觉。我们都为你加油。正是如此。我们为我们自己加油，我们互相支持。

turns.en: You know, we want to see good returns and it's, we're part of the essence. So we needed to have this as part of the, you know, the tripod and there were other things we needed to do.
turns.zh: 我们想看到好回报，我们就是这份事业本质的一部分。所以我们需要把这作为那三足鼎立的一足，还有别的我们也需要做到。

turns.en: But we needed to be part of the essence of Goldman Sachs, especially as we got bigger. You've run a lot of investment committee meetings in your career and you once told me that it's okay to disagree, but you can't be disagreeable.
turns.zh: 但我们需要成为 Goldman Sachs 本质的一部分，尤其当我们越做越大之后。你职业生涯里主持过很多次投资委员会，你曾跟我说过：可以有分歧，但你不能讨人嫌（disagreeable）。

turns.en: Right. So what does that mean? So it means a lot to me. I'll say this way. We run a very, and we still do a very, what I'll call honest investment committee process, which means people speak up.
turns.zh: 没错。那这是什么意思？这对我意义重大。我这么说吧：我们运行的——到今天仍然是——一个我非常愿意称之为'诚实'的投资委员会流程，也就是人们会开口说话。

turns.en: And I don't care how young of a partner you are or whatever, people, it's a forum to come in and give you reviews and give your ideas. We have to have decorum, but I don't want to silence the input because we have so many smart people here.
turns.zh: 我不在乎你是多年轻的合伙人，或别的什么——这是一个你进来发表意见、贡献想法的论坛。我们要有礼节（decorum），但我不想压制输入，因为我们有这么多聪明人在这儿。

turns.en: So it seemed to me that we want to bait. We want people to say, this doesn't make any sense to me. Explain to me why, you know, how does this really work and do it in an open fashion?
turns.zh: 所以在我看来，我们要鼓励大家说：'这对我来说说不通，给我解释一下这到底怎么运作'，而且要以公开的方式去做。

turns.en: That's where I adopted this phrase and, you know, it was, I'll copyright it is, it's okay to disagree. You can disagree and you can disagree with force, but you can't be disagreeable.
turns.zh: 我就是在那时候采纳了这句话——我要给它注上版权——'可以有分歧。你可以持不同意见，可以强烈地反对，但你不能讨人嫌。'

turns.en: Well, you can't be in there acting like a jerk and creating that kind of negative, you know, vibes in the room because that's going to then spiral because then others will do the same.
turns.zh: 你不能在那儿像个混蛋一样表现，营造出那种负面的氛围，因为那会形成恶性循环，然后别人也会照样做。

turns.en: And I think the people get it. I never thought it was smart to create investment committees where the chairman of the investment committee made all the calls without all the relevant input.
turns.zh: 我想大家都能理解。我从来都不觉得，让一个投资委员会里主席一个人、在没有充分听取各方意见的情况下拍板所有决定，是明智的。

turns.en: And I would never, we'd never approved deals if it was like 60, 40, or 55, 45, if you counted heads. We wanted a strong consensus of support for any investment that we made.
turns.zh: 如果按人头算是六十比四十、五十五比四十五，我们从来不会批准交易。我们要求对任何一笔投资都有强烈的共识支持。

turns.en: And I just believe that we had really smart people and that as small as we are, you know, this is particularly the future. It's like, we're not so good at this.
turns.zh: 我只是相信我们的人真的很聪明，而哪怕我们规模还小——尤其在关乎未来的时候——也不能说我们在这方面就那么在行。

turns.en: And so it's like, you know, let's get enough support and reasons why and then we can make the call. And today we've taken it to the next level.
turns.zh: 所以我们会说：先取得足够的支持、弄清理由，然后我们再做决定。而到今天，我们把它提升到了更高的层次。

turns.en: We have an incredible group helping us think this through. So I think it's, I was never afraid of opinions. I wanted the opinions, but I didn't want, you know, antagonism, you know, in that room.
turns.zh: 我们有一支了不起的团队在帮我们把这些想透。所以我从来不害怕意见分歧，我想要那些观点，但我不想要那个房间里的敌意（antagonism）。

turns.en: And I think everyone got it. And it was a small enough committee that everyone understood it and there was enough experience in there that, and people believe they said, okay, we like this model.
turns.zh: 我想大家都明白了。而且委员会足够小，人人都理解这套做法，里面也足够有经验，以至于大家会说：好，我们喜欢这个模式。

turns.en: It makes sense. No, that's smart. How have you balanced consistent performance and staying true to your principles? And was there ever a time that those two things were at odds?
turns.zh: 这说得通。没错，很聪明。你是如何在'保持一贯的业绩'和'忠于你的原则'之间取得平衡的？这两者之间，有没有过冲突的时候？

turns.en: Oh, yeah. I mean, there are odds now. I mean, whenever you go through these moments and periods, you know, everyone's like wondering, you know, I mean, it goes back to the late 90s, like, you know, how come you're not in AOL or how come you're not in Netscape?
turns.zh: 哦，有。我是说，现在就有。每当你经历这样的时刻和时期，所有人都会疑惑——这又要回到九十年代末那种：'你为什么没投 AOL？为什么没投 Netscape？'

turns.en: And why aren't we in those deals? And the same thing will go on now, which is if you're not active in AI right now, you know, you're useless.
turns.zh: 我们为什么没参与那些交易？而同样的事现在还会再来——如果你现在不在 AI 上活跃，你就是没用了。

turns.en: So it's sort of like, you know, you have to sort of balance that, which is how aggressive do we want to be during momentum periods? Consistency and staying within what we're good at has proven to be true.
turns.zh: 所以多少要在那之间取得平衡，也就是：在动量（momentum）时期，我们想多激进？'保持一致、待在我们擅长的领域里'，已经被证明是对的。

turns.en: And that means you're going to miss some things, but we really haven't historically been that successful by, you know, jumping on the momentum thing and being at the top.
turns.zh: 这意味着你会错过一些东西，但从历史上看，靠跟风动量、追在顶端，我们其实没那么成功。

turns.en: Because those things, they crash. But sometimes what we would do is we would temper them. So I remember, you know, with the tech of the 2000 period, you know, there was all this pressure to do tech and tech telecom at the time.
turns.zh: 因为那些东西会崩盘。但有时候我们会做的是给它们降降温。我记得 2000 年那波科技的时候，当时有巨大的压力要去做科技和电信（telecom）。

turns.en: And we were like, uh, so about five or 600 million of that fund sort of got invested in tech and telecom. And then, but that was 10%. And then it sort of like faded, went away.
turns.zh: 我们就——嗯，那只基金里大概有五六亿美元投到了科技和电信。但那也就占 10%。然后它就慢慢淡出、过去了。

turns.en: And it didn't kill the fund, but we at least were playing at it. And there were times we've had to say no, we decided there were places that were off limits.
turns.zh: 它没有搞垮基金，但至少我们参与过。有些时候我们也不得不说不——我们认定有些地方是禁区。

turns.en: We didn't have to go to every part of the world. We had plenty of opportunity in our home territories that we defined as home territories. So we stayed within our geographic, you know, places of US, Europe, Asia, which is plenty.
turns.zh: 我们不必去到世界每一个角落。在我们界定的'本土市场'（home territories）里有足够多的机会。所以我们待在我们的地理范围里：美国、欧洲、亚洲，这就够多了。

turns.en: And then we, we struggled through those periods of momentum. They're really hard because if you're not active in them, you look like you're, you know, you're just at a place.
turns.zh: 然后我们熬过了那些动量时期。它们真的很难，因为如果你不参与，你看起来就像——原地不动、落于人后。

turns.en: You talked earlier about starting the first subordinated debt fund. Private markets have obviously grown massively over the past decades. So has that made it harder or easier for you to find opportunities?
turns.zh: 你之前提到发起了第一只次级债基金。过去几十年私募市场显然巨幅增长了。那么，这让你寻找机会变得更难了，还是更容易了？

turns.en: I've always felt that competition on the private equity side where we play has always been intense. Because it really only takes one other, you know, party to, to create a very, you know, competitive, you know, circumstance.
turns.zh: 我始终觉得，我们玩的那块私募股权一侧的竞争一直都很激烈。因为往往只要有那么一个其他对手，就能制造出非常、非常竞争激烈的局面。

turns.en: I never imagined the PE industry would evolve into what it is, right? It just, being a pioneer is like looking at this and saying, oh my God, this is industrialized.
turns.zh: 我从没想过 PE 行业会演变成今天这样。就是，作为一个先行者，看着眼前这一切会说：天哪，这已经工业化了。

turns.en: There are hundreds and hundreds of them. Thousands and thousands of them. What's happening in our sweet spots is when there are businesses for sale, there seems to be only like two to three or four that really pay attention and get involved.
turns.zh: 有几百几千家，几千家。我们最擅长的领域里发生的是：当有企业待售时，看起来真正关注并参与的也就那么两到四家。

turns.en: And that's because there's so much activity that you can't look at everything. So I think at least right now, yeah, we just bought, you know, signed a couple of deals in the last, you know, week or so.
turns.zh: 这是因为活动太多，你不可能什么都看得到。所以我想至少眼下——我们刚在过去差不多一周里签了几笔交易。

turns.en: These were mid-sized companies, which is, which is our sweet spot. And they really wanted to other competitors. There weren't 10 or 20 because no one wants to be in something where you have to pay for due diligence and spend $2 million against 10 other people.
turns.zh: 这些都是中等规模的公司，正是我们的甜点区（sweet spot）。它们其实并没有引来很多别的竞争者——不是十家二十家，因为没人愿意参与一桩你得付尽调费、要和另外十个人抢、砸两百万的项目。

turns.en: So it's sort of a strange world in that sense. I think it's always been competitive. It's a lousy industry from a standpoint of looking at how many players, how much money, how much opportunity.
turns.zh: 所以从某种意义上说，这是个挺奇怪的世界。我想它一直都是竞争激烈的。如果你去看有多少玩家、多少钱、多少机会，从某个角度看这是个'糟透了'的行业。

turns.en: But it's an incredible, you know, business to be able to go search, find, and then manage and create. And the question is, you know, is that still doable in the world?
turns.zh: 但它又是一门了不起的生意——能去搜寻、发现，然后管理、创造。问题是，在这世界上这还行得通吗？

turns.en: And my answer would be, yeah, it's a much bigger world. But I never imagined, you know, we'd have an industry with thousands of competitors, three to five trillion of assets in inventory, the needing to find a home.
turns.zh: 我的答案是：行得通，只是世界大多了。但我从没想过，我们会拥有一个有几千家竞争对手、有三到五万亿美元资产等着找归属的行业。

turns.en: I would have never imagined. What I'd say is, and this goes back to 2005, when I'll say what I'm going to say, or six or seven, something like that.
turns.zh: 我绝想不到。要说我想讲的一点，得回到 2005、或者 2006、07 年左右。

turns.en: We sit with our senior team and we say, OK, we're only going to make five to seven investments a year. We could have a great business with five to seven decent sized investments a year.
turns.zh: 我们和高级团队坐下来，说：好，我们一年只做五到七笔投资。哪怕一年只做五到七笔像样的投资，也能是一门好生意。

turns.en: And that's the same thing today, which is there's plenty to do. People have plenty of their portfolio companies to be involved with. But we're not trying to conquer the world.
turns.zh: 而今天也一样——有的是事可做。人们对自家组合里的公司有足够多要操心的。但我们并不是要征服世界。

turns.en: And let's think about that in terms of the Warren Buffett idea that you have just a certain amount of punches on your ticket that you can have, which is, is this one of the five, six, or seven?
turns.zh: 这可以用 Warren Buffett 的那个想法来理解：你的人生投票卡上只有有限的几次出手额度——这笔，是不是那五、六、七次之一？

turns.en: So I think we're seeing enough, but it's a very complicated world. So you're in the middle of your fifth decade investing and leading. I was going to say, I think I'm in the middle of my sixth decade living, but yeah, or seventh decade.
turns.zh: 所以我想我们看到的机会足够多了，但这是个非常复杂的世界。你现在正处在投资和领导生涯的第五个十年。我本来想说，我觉得我正处在人生的第六个十年——不过是啊，或者第七个。

turns.en: No, but fifth decade investing, having built the Merchant Bank over so many decades. And you've invested through multiple crises, bubbles, as we've talked about, and market regimes.
turns.zh: 不，是投资的第五个十年——在这么多年里建起了商户银行。而你穿越过多次危机、泡沫，就像我们谈到的，以及各种市场周期（market regimes）。

turns.en: What event in your view tested you most in your career? And what did you learn from that? I think the event that sort of was the biggest shock was the great financial crisis, if you will, because no one knew anything.
turns.zh: 在你看来，哪一件事在你的职业生涯里对你考验最大？你从中学到了什么？我想最让人震惊的那件事，应该是全球金融危机（Great Financial Crisis）——因为当时谁都摸不着头脑。

turns.en: And Goldman Sachs was having an existential moment, if you will. The common view was, because you knew this, was that there was all these, there was just a wall of debt financings that wasn't going to happen, and every private equity investment was going to fail.
turns.zh: Goldman Sachs 当时正经历一个存亡攸关的时刻。普遍的共识是——你也知道——有一大堵墙的债务融资不会发生，每一笔私募股权投资都会失败。

turns.en: You know, that didn't happen, obviously. And more than once in my career have we been forced to go to our portfolio at large, all of the companies, and say, there's a problem.
turns.zh: 显然，那并没有发生。在我的职业生涯里，我们不止一次被迫向整个组合、所有公司喊话：出问题了。

turns.en: You're going to have a financing issue. We're going to have to batten down the hatches. We're going to have to do this and do that. And, you know, that's happened more than more than a few times.
turns.zh: 你们会遇到融资困难，我们得关紧舱盖、各就各位，得这么做、那么做。这种事发生过的次数，不止寥寥几次。

turns.en: And so, you know, there is a, there is enough of a crisis history to know that these things, you know, come around periodically. But I think that probably was the most scary at the moment.
turns.zh: 所以危机史已经足够多，让人知道这类事情会周期性地卷土重来。但我想，那一刻大概是最可怕的。

turns.en: And as Lloyd would say, you know, today's crisis is worse than that crisis because that crisis is over. So, you know, I'd say, you know, the crisis today in the PE industry is exits.
turns.zh: 正如 Lloyd 会说的那样：今天的危机比那次更糟，因为那次危机已经过去了。所以我会说——PE 行业今天的危机是退出（exits）。

turns.en: It's not operating performance. Operating performance is probably, you know, as good as it could be over, you know, your whole portfolio. But how do you exit your investments?
turns.zh: 不是经营表现。经营表现大概在整个组合里都算是能有多好就有多好了。但你怎么退出你的投资？

turns.en: And I think that, you know, the public market and the strategic market aren't going to be big buyers of the lion's share of the inventory, if you will.
turns.zh: 我想，公开市场和战略买家不会成为这批存货（inventory）大部分的大买家。

turns.en: So that's going to be a really interesting thing to see over time. How, you know, how maybe there'll be industrial transactions with PE firms together and then exits.
turns.zh: 所以随着时间推移，这会是一个非常值得观察的看点——也许会看到 PE 公司之间联手做产业交易，然后才谈退出。

turns.en: But it's going to be a, everything's slowed. Yep. Let's put it that way. In the year over year, M&A stats in, you know, corporate world and tech versus PE.
turns.zh: 但总之，一切都慢了下来。是的，就这么说吧。看同比的并购（M&A）数据——企业界和科技界 vs PE。

turns.en: From an overall investment perspective, what are you excited about today? What are the things that excite you most at investment committee? What you're seeing around the world?
turns.zh: 从整体投资的角度来看，你今天对什么感到兴奋？在投资委员会上，最让你兴奋的是什么？你在世界各地看到了什么？

turns.en: You know, I'd say that the, it's funny, it's the excitement isn't where the action is. Because where the action is, that excitement has valuations that are, we can't even ponder.
turns.zh: 你知道，有意思的是——让人兴奋的地方，往往不是热闹所在的地方。因为热闹所在之处，那些估值是我们连想都不敢想的。

turns.en: I mean, I thought we saw it all in 2000, but these are multiples of a hundred times that. There was no talk of colonizing Mars back in 2000 or everyone's going to have a robot and, you know, all these kind of different things that, you know, happened on the Jetsons that everyone thinks is going to happen.
turns.zh: 我本以为 2000 年我们把一切见尽了，但那些估值是当年的上百倍。2000 年可没人说要殖民火星，或者人人都会有个机器人、各种《杰森一家》（The Jetsons）里那种大家都以为会实现的事。

turns.en: Not all of our viewers will even remember the Jetsons. But I'd say the things that have been more interesting for us in sort of the 500 million to a billion and a half range have been wealth management.
turns.zh: 并非我们所有的观众都还记得《杰森一家》。但我会说，对我们来说更有意思的，是在大约五亿到十五亿美元那个区间里的一些方向，比如财富管理（wealth management）。

turns.en: There are more wealthy people looking for, you know, ways to invest their money. And this has been, you know, somewhat in Europe, you know, accounting for, I mean, business services, I guess, is what I would say, maybe stands out the most.
turns.zh: 越来越多的富裕人群在寻找投资自己财富的方式。而这，某种程度上——尤其是在欧洲——要我说，最突出的大概是商业服务（business services）。

turns.en: I'd rather be servicing the infrastructure that's being put into the data centers than necessarily owning these data centers. Because if four trillion gets invested over the next three plus years to what's been invested, could that have a good return?
turns.zh: 我宁愿去服务那些正被建进数据中心的基础设施，也不一定要拥有这些数据中心本身。因为如果未来三年多时间里要投入四万亿美元，相比已经投进去的，这还能有好回报吗？

turns.en: I mean, it's just those numbers are just so big. I mean, it's fascinating. You know, by recent data shows, employment's up. So it's like it's not taking away jobs yet.
turns.zh: 我是说，这些数字实在太大了，太迷人了。最新数据显示就业在上升，所以至少到现在还没夺走工作机会。

turns.en: But again, that's a big yes. So it's a very complicated world. I am not a technologist. I'm not a visionary. And it's like this has been, you know, there's no doubt AI is the most hyped of anything I've ever seen in our business careers.
turns.zh: 但同样，那是个大大的未知数。所以这是个非常复杂的世界。我不是技术专家，也不是有远见的人。这件事，毫不夸张地说，AI 是我在职业生涯里见过的被炒得最热的一样东西。

turns.en: Now, it has capabilities that we've never seen before. But the history of others is they underperform that. They don't quite work out as we think.
turns.zh: 如今它有着我们前所未见的能力。但过往其他技术史的经验是，它们的表现不及预期，没完全像我们以为的那样成功。

turns.en: So it's sort of like, we'll see. And it's going to take a long time to prove out because soon after the tech bubble thing, the only thing we had was we had email.
turns.zh: 所以多少是'走着瞧'。而要证明出来会需要很长时间，因为在科技泡沫之后，我们真正拥有的只有邮件。

turns.en: We had package services, package goods were delivered by Amazon. And we had a few other things. And then 20 years later, a lot of the stuff that was promised back then, you know, is here.
turns.zh: 我们有了包裹服务，亚马逊（Amazon）帮我们送包裹，还有那么几样别的东西。二十年后，当年承诺的一大堆东西才真正落地。

turns.en: So technology is the force that's driving most. But I think we do better in sort of like, in niche businesses that we can, you know, invest in and buy and grow with it.
turns.zh: 所以科技是驱动最多的那股力量。但我想，我们更擅长的，是那种我们既能投资、又能买下、还能一起成长的细分生意。

turns.en: I love the sports businesses. We can't, we're not going to own teams. But I think the servicing, you know, services to, you know, to the sports, I think that continues to be a growing area.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢体育这门生意。我们不会去拥有球队。但我认为面向体育的服务——那会是一个持续增长的领域。

turns.en: You know, the general economy in the U.S. is okay. Without AI, it's not okay. But with AI, it's okay. We're open for business. We're not going to go crazy.
turns.zh: 你知道，美国整体经济还行。要是没有 AI，那就不行；有了 AI，就还行。我们开门营业，但我们不会疯狂下注。

turns.en: But it's complicated. Yep. So speaking of sports, sports has been a huge part of your life personally. Not only did you play college basketball at Brown, but you've played a long-running regular game with many colleagues at Goldman Sachs on the Upper East Side.
turns.zh: 但事情很复杂。是的。说到体育——体育在你个人生活里一直是很重要的一部分。你不只是在 Brown 打过大学篮球，你还在上东区（Upper East Side）和 Goldman Sachs 的许多同事一起打了一场持续多年的固定球局。

turns.en: So what has basketball taught you about both discipline as well as investing? What you said is 100% true. Sports has been very important to me throughout.
turns.zh: 那篮球教会了你什么关于纪律、也关于投资的东西？你说的百分之百对。体育对我来说一直非常重要。

turns.en: And fortunately, no surgeries on anything here. Yeah, I know. I've said it so many times that I've exhausted that superstition. The basketball team was the old, and I missed that.
turns.zh: 幸运的是，我这儿什么都没做过手术。是啊，我知道。这话我说太多遍，把这个迷信都用尽了。篮球队那批是老队伍了，我很怀念。

turns.en: I stopped seven years ago because I was afraid it would get hurt. But there's the teamwork. There's the understanding of strategy. There's collaboration.
turns.zh: 我七年前就停了，因为我怕受伤。但那里有团队合作，有对策略的理解，有协作。

turns.en: You know, there's a lot of things that are interactive with things to know when you want the ball, when somebody else gets the ball. So I think there are elements of that that fostered, you know, working together in an environment with others.
turns.zh: 有很多互动的东西——什么时候你要球、什么时候让别人拿球。所以我觉得那些元素，培养了你和他人共事、在一个环境里一起协作的能力。

turns.en: You know, in contrast to the individual sports where the person can be unbelievable, but they might not necessarily have the same, you know, interconnectivity.
turns.zh: 相比之下，个人项目里，那个人可以非常出色，但未必有同样的那种相互联结。

turns.en: In terms of the investing, where I got my best elements was when I was growing up, I would be going to the racetrack. I'd be playing cards. I'd be even going to bingo games if necessary.
turns.zh: 在投资这方面，我最好的养分来自小时候——我会去跑马场，会打牌，必要的话还去 bingo 游戏。

turns.en: When I was in my teens, it was the most fun thing we could do. We were little in the young side, but they accepted us there. But I think I learned more about money management and reading people than anything else.
turns.zh: 我十几岁的时候，那是最好玩的事。我们年纪小、偏年幼，但他们接纳我们。我想，关于资金管理和察人观心，我从那里学到的比什么都多。

turns.en: So that brings us to your philanthropy efforts, which are actually pretty wide-ranging. So what are your current priorities there? So philanthropy has been really important.
turns.zh: 那这就说到你的慈善事业（philanthropy）了，其实范围相当广。你现在的优先关注是什么？慈善真的非常重要。

turns.en: First of all, I think that I think all the sacks brought it into my DNA because I didn't really have that before I got here. You know, what I did over time is we did have a strategy, and the strategy was around, and it followed the kids and it followed our lives.
turns.zh: 首先，我想是 Goldman Sachs 把慈善放进了我的 DNA，因为我来这儿之前其实并没有这种意识。我随着时间做的是，我们确有一套战略，而这套战略是跟着孩子走、跟着我们的生活走的。

turns.en: You know, it followed Jewish causes, health care, education. And on the education side, it sort of followed where we went to school and where the kids went to school.
turns.zh: 它跟着犹太事业（Jewish causes）、医疗保健、教育走。在教育这块，它大致跟着我们上过的学校、孩子们上过的学校走。

turns.en: But I've concentrated in the last 10 years, you know, with education with Brown, and I did receive a doctorate degree there. So somebody asked me, well, how much did that cost?
turns.zh: 但过去十年，我把重心放在教育上，尤其是 Brown，我还在那儿拿到了一个荣誉博士学位。有人问我：那花了多少钱？

turns.en: I said, yeah, it was much more expensive than my earlier degree. But no, but congratulations. That was really great. Mount Sinai has been very important.
turns.zh: 我说：是啊，那比我早年的学位贵多了。不过——恭喜你，那真的很棒。Mount Sinai 也一直非常重要。

turns.en: And I just finished my term as a coach here there, and I felt like we did a really good job. And then Jewish causes. And right now, that's probably the time that one thing I'm devoting most time to is fighting anti-Semitism in Palm Beach County.
turns.zh: 我刚在那儿结束了一任董事会主席的任期，我觉得我们做得非常出色。然后是犹太事业。眼下，可能有一件我投入最多时间的事，就是在 Palm Beach 县对抗反犹太主义（anti-Semitism）。

turns.en: It's not a national campaign. This is just in the region. We've gotten the whole oil of Palm Beach County. We've gotten great support financially.
turns.zh: 这不是全国性的运动，只是在这个地区。我们已经让 Palm Beach 县的各界都参与进来，在资金上也得到了很好的支持。

turns.en: And I think we've built up, you know, a good program, but it's really regional. And I think there'll be more things that, you know, that occur to me.
turns.zh: 我想我们搭建起了一个不错的计划，但它确实是区域性的。以后我还会想到更多要去做的事。

turns.en: But it's like, you know, the three top ones are 95% of really where we've devoted our time and wealth assets. And the rest are being supported, if you will.
turns.zh: 但就像，排前三的那几项，真正占了我们投入的时间和财富资产的百分之九十五。其余的也在被支持着。

turns.en: But I think it's important. I think it's, and when people say, where did you get it from? I say, I got it from Goldman Sachs. Tell me a little bit more about that.
turns.zh: 但我觉得这很重要。当人们问'你这套是从哪儿来的'，我说：我是从 Goldman Sachs 那儿学来的。

turns.en: When did you get it from Goldman Sachs? And how did you get it from Goldman Sachs? Well, the funny thing was, and I'm sure you had your own story about this, was I think I was a first year or second year associate.
turns.zh: 再多讲讲这个吧。你是从 Goldman Sachs 什么时候、怎么学来的？有意思的是——我相信你自己也有类似的故事——我想那时候我大概是一年级或二年级的 associate。

turns.en: And all of a sudden Steve Friedman walks around and goes, okay, Friedman, O'Toole, Mira, go! You're all going up to the UJA event, the card calling event.
turns.zh: 突然 Steve Friedman 走过来喊：好，Friedman、O'Toole、Mira，走！你们全都上去参加 UJA 的活动，那个电话募捐（card calling）活动。

turns.en: And, you know, we're there. You know, we're making nothing. And all of a sudden it's like, Ace Greenberg is $500,000. You know, Steve Friedman gives a million dollars.
turns.zh: 我们就在那儿，你知道，我们一分不赚。然后突然——Ace Greenberg 捐了五十万美元，Steve Friedman 捐了一百万美元。

turns.en: And we're like sitting there saying, we're going under the table. So we learned early on that ultimately being supportive is important. But it took, it took, it takes a while, you know, to really sort of think about what you want to be supportive of, what you want to be involved with and why.
turns.zh: 我们就坐在那儿想：我们要钻桌子底下了。所以我们很早就学到——归根结底，给予支持很重要。但要真正想清楚你想支持什么、想参与什么、以及为什么，需要好一段时间。

turns.en: And everyone has to come up with their own strategy for it. So over the course of your 45 year tenure at the firm, obviously Goldman Sachs has changed in a lot of ways.
turns.zh: 每个人都得拿出自己的一套战略。在你为这家公司效力的四十五年里，Goldman Sachs 显然在很多方面都变了。

turns.en: You've mentioned some of that, but what has stayed the same in your view over those decades? I believe and I'd like to believe, but I'm not, you know, in these offices every day is the pride that people have in being here.
turns.zh: 你提到了一些，那在你看来，在这几十年里有什么始终没变？我相信——我希望如此——虽然我不天天待在那些办公室里，但人们身为其中一员的那份自豪感。

turns.en: The collaboration that, you know, people have here. The, you know, the focus on winning and success in the context of what our strategy is. And then the trust that people have in the organization, because it is very different.
turns.zh: 人们之间的协作，在'赢'和'成功'上的专注——放在我们的战略背景里去看——以及人们对这个组织的信任。因为它真的非常不同。

turns.en: I mean, you know, simple metrics, when I joined, there were 2000 people. We had 200 million of capital. You know, it was, it was very, very different, you know, kind of a place.
turns.zh: 我是说，几个简单的指标：我加入时只有两千人，我们有两亿美元的资本。那是一个极其、极其不同的地方。

turns.en: And you didn't really know much about what was going on. You know, here, obviously we have 50,000 people, 300 billion market cap. And, you know, the, the, I think the challenge for people today is, you know, where do they fit?
turns.zh: 当时你也了解不到多少正在发生什么。而如今，显然我们有五万人、三千亿美元的市值。我想今天人们面对的挑战是：我在这儿的位置在哪里？

turns.en: And where can they make a difference? Because the places. So, I mean, I felt when I joined, oh my God, how could I ever be successful? There's so many people here.
turns.zh: 我能在哪里发挥作用？因为地方太大了。所以，我加入时我会想：天哪，这么多人，我怎么可能成功？

turns.en: Now if you join, you just say, oh my God, 50,000 people, 300 billion market cap. You know, what can I ever do to make a difference here? But I think it's, it's the, it's the camaraderie.
turns.zh: 现在你要是加入，你会说：天哪，五万人，三千亿市值，我能在这里做出什么名堂？但我想，那份情谊（camaraderie）——

turns.en: It's the collaboration. It's the feeling like you're part of the winning team. It's been an incredible personal platform because the people and the relationships you have here, as well as outside, creates a very fulfilling, you know, existence, you know, for you if you, if you do it right.
turns.zh: 那份协作，那种'你是赢家团队一员'的感觉——它是一个非常了不起的个人平台。因为这里以及这里之外的人和关系，如果你做得好，会成就一段非常充实的人生。

turns.en: So my last question before we go to our lightning round, what is the key to succeeding in today's environment and economy, both as an employee of Goldman Sachs and as an investor?
turns.zh: 那我们进入快问快答（lightning round）之前的最后一个问题：在今天的环境和经济里，无论作为 Goldman Sachs 的员工，还是作为投资人，成功的关键是什么？

turns.en: You know, a lot of ways today is so different. In other ways, it's the same. And success only comes before work in the dictionary. You got to put the work in.
turns.zh: 你知道，今天的很多方面是截然不同的，而在其他一些方面又一样。成功这个词，只有在字典里才排在'努力'前面。你得下苦功。

turns.en: You got to be committed. And, you know, you can't, you know, get there by, you know, sort of like without doing the heavy lifting. I've always felt that people have to like, you know, contribute and also think.
turns.zh: 你得全身心投入。你不能不干重活就想抵达终点。我始终觉得，人们既要贡献，也要思考。

turns.en: I always think about when they're working on an assignment, it's not just a task. It's like, well, understand what you're doing and then, you know, contextualize it and be able to sort of like make, have an opinion about whether this makes sense or be a participant in that project or task.
turns.zh: 我总在想，当他们做一个任务时，那不仅仅是一项差事，而是：理解你在做什么，把它放进情境里，能够形成观点——判断这件事说不说得通，或者成为那个项目、任务中一个有想法的参与者。

turns.en: I still think the career opportunities at Goldman Sachs are outstanding. And maybe the paths that were interesting before are different today.
turns.zh: 我仍然觉得 Goldman Sachs 的职业机会是出类拔萃的。也许以前吸引人的路径，今天有所不同。

turns.en: So you have to sort of investigate that. And you have to have good relationships with people. Because if you're a talented person, someone's going to, you know, tap their hand, you know, on your shoulder, like, you know, like I'd had or you had and say, I want you to do this.
turns.zh: 所以你得自己去研究。你还得和别人处好关系。因为如果你是个有才华的人，总会有人拍拍你的肩膀，就像别人对我、对你做过的那样，说：我要你去做这件事。

turns.en: And maybe that, you know, leads to something that could be interesting. But look, Goldman Sachs has become a juggernaut and it's really fantastic.
turns.zh: 也许那就会通向你觉得有意思的东西。但你看，Goldman Sachs 已经成了一个巨头，这真的很了不起。

turns.en: All right, so I'd like to end these conversations with a lightning round. What would you say is your greatest strength as an investor? Being able to pull all the information together and have a let's call it strategic view of where this is going to go and whether or not this is going to really work or not.
turns.zh: 好，我想用一个快问快答来结束这些对话。作为投资人，你觉得自己最大的优点是什么？——能够把所有信息汇聚起来，形成一种姑且称之为战略性的视野，判断它会走向哪里、到底行不行得通。

turns.en: I think we're all good at looking down. We're not so good at looking out. And I think I'm pretty good at looking out over the horizon. What is the best piece of advice you've ever received?
turns.zh: 我想我们都善于往低处看，但不太善于往远处看。而我想，我还挺善于眺望远方地平线的。你收到过的最好的一条建议是什么？

turns.en: Okay, so this this is going to take me back 60 plus years. I don't remember, you know, exactly. But my father told me if you're going to do something, do it right.
turns.zh: 好，这会把我带回六十多年前。我不太记得确切的了，但我父亲跟我说过：要做一件事，就把它做对。

turns.en: It's good advice. Similar to something my father said. How do you spend your time outside of the office now? So I become a golf fanatic. You know, I play way too much.
turns.zh: 这是句好建议，跟我父亲说过的挺像。你现在不在办公室的时候都怎么打发时间？——结果我成了个高尔夫狂迷，打得实在太多了。

turns.en: It's my happy place right now. So if I have free time, I'm out on that golf course. I've gotten okay. I'm not going to ever be great because I never learned how to hit when I was young.
turns.zh: 它现在是我的快乐天地。所以只要我有空，我就在高尔夫球场上。我打得还行了，永远成不了高手，因为我小时候没学过怎么挥杆。

turns.en: But I could play with everybody and I have a lot of fun and it's put you outside and sunny. And you know, this is something that everyone has to figure out.
turns.zh: 但我能和任何人一起打，我玩得非常开心，它让你待在户外、晒着太阳。这是每个人都得为自己找到的一样东西。

turns.en: Okay, what's going to be those next chapters? Right. This is filled in for me from a sports standpoint and a time standpoint that I have it because my kids are grandkids are up here.
turns.zh: 好，那接下来的篇章会是什么？——对我来说，这一块在运动和可支配时间上已经被填满了，因为我的孩子、孙辈们都在北边。

turns.en: We're down in Florida. So you need to fill that schedule. So that's sort of that's my happy place. Which investor do you admire most? I'm not going to glorify anyone currently because I'm not going to help them raise a fund.
turns.zh: 我们在南边的 Florida，所以你得把日程填满——那大概就是我的快乐天地。你最钦佩的投资人是谁？——我不打算抬举任何一个还在世的人，因为我不想帮他们募资。

turns.en: And maybe I should think about someone who's not alive because that makes it easier. But if I thought back in time to some of the people I met, I didn't get to know all that well.
turns.zh: 也许我该想一个已经不在了的人，那样更容易些。但如果回想我遇到过的某些人——我并没有和他们那么熟。

turns.en: But I got inspired by him. It was Richard Rainwater. And I met him in a lunch at Goldman Sachs for the first time. And then we brought him back to do a seminar with our team, if you will.
turns.zh: 但我从他身上受到过激励，那就是 Richard Rainwater。我第一次是在 Goldman Sachs 的一顿午餐上见到他，后来我们把他又请来，跟我们的团队做了一场分享。

turns.en: And I just sort of, you know, I never really got to know him that well. But I heard really good things about him in terms of how he lived his life and what he did.
turns.zh: 我只是——我其实没怎么深入了解过他。但我听了很多关于他的好评——关于他怎样度过他的一生、做过些什么。

turns.en: But I thought that he was a, if I was a pioneer, he was a, you know, he was even before that, a pretty special guy. All right. And finally, what are you most excited about in the world right now?
turns.zh: 但我觉得，如果说我是个先行者，他比我更早，是个非常特别的人。好，最后一个问题：眼下在这个世界上，你最兴奋的是什么？

turns.en: If you saw my six year old grandson backhand, it's unbelievable, Alice. And this kid, you know, it's an incredible backhand. You know, I think it's a challenging world right now.
turns.zh: 如果你看过我六岁孙子的反手（backhand），那真是不可思议，Allison。这孩子——他有一记了不起的反手。我想现在是个充满挑战的世界。

turns.en: It really is. And challenging also can make it very interesting. I don't know where he is taking us. I know everyone is so optimistic about all the things that, you know, could happen.
turns.zh: 确实如此。而挑战也能让它变得非常有意思。我不知道它要把我们带向何方。我知道所有人都对那些可能发生的事无比乐观。

turns.en: And yeah, maybe they could happen, but I don't think they're going to be happening on the time frame that everybody sort of thinks. You know, it's certainly not a dull period, but it's a scary period.
turns.zh: 是啊，也许那些真会发生，但我不认为它们会按照大家以为的那个时间表发生。这确实不是一个乏味的时期，但它是个令人不安的时期。

turns.en: It is. So there's a lot of things that are troubling. We just got to keep putting one foot in front of the other and keep going. That's true.
turns.zh: 是啊。有很多事情令人忧虑。我们只能一步接一步地往前走，继续下去。没错。

turns.en: Well, I was trying to end on a positive note, so. Let's talk about it. Go back to your grandson. That's right. It's backhand. That's his backhand.
turns.zh: 我本想以一个积极的调子收尾的。那我们就聊聊这个吧，回到你孙子。对，那是他的反手——他的反手。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Anyway, well, thank you so much, Reggie. Thank you, Alice. This was a lot of fun. This is great. This is great. And I got dressed up for it, too.
turns.zh: 正是如此。总之，真的非常感谢你，Rich。谢谢你，Allison。这太有趣了，太棒了——我还特意穿了正装来录呢。

turns.en: You did. You look amazing. I was expecting the golf shirt. Thank you all for listening to this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges, Great Investors, which was recorded on Tuesday, July 28th, 2026.
turns.zh: 你确实穿了，你看起来精神极了。我还以为你会穿件高尔夫球衫呢。感谢大家收听本期 Goldman Sachs Exchanges 的《Great Investors》，本集录制于 2026 年 7 月 28 日，星期二。
